title: Decoupling Legacy Content Delivery via Reverse Proxy
business: A regional archival library maintaining a legacy document repository that lacks modern security headers and encryption support.
problem: The legacy repository runs on an internal server without TLS capabilities, exposing sensitive historical documents to cleartext interception when accessed by remote researchers.
solution: Deploying Apache HTTP Server as a reverse proxy layer. By placing Apache in front of the legacy server, the organization can terminate SSL/TLS connections at the proxy, inject required security headers, and forward requests to the internal repository over a secure tunnel, shielding the legacy infrastructure from direct exposure.
steps: Install the Apache HTTP Server with mod_proxy and mod_ssl modules enabled.
Configure a VirtualHost to listen on port 443 with valid SSL certificates.
Define ProxyPass and ProxyPassReverse directives to map public requests to the internal legacy server IP.
Use Header directives to inject security policies like Strict-Transport-Security.
Restart the service to apply the proxy configuration and verify the secure handshake.
outcome: Researchers can access historical documents via encrypted HTTPS connections, while the legacy repository remains isolated from direct public network traffic.
limitation: The primary limitation is the increased latency introduced by the proxy hop and the potential for the proxy to become a single point of failure. Administrators can check for this by monitoring the Apache error logs and using system-level tools to track connection timeouts between the proxy and the backend server.

questions.question: In Decoupling Legacy Content Delivery via Reverse Proxy, how does the solution address the security risk?
options: By replacing the legacy server entirely with Apache.
By terminating SSL/TLS at the proxy and shielding the internal server.
By encrypting the files directly on the legacy server disk.
By forcing researchers to use a VPN instead of HTTPS.
questions.explanation: The solution explicitly mentions using the proxy to terminate SSL/TLS and shield the legacy infrastructure.
questions.evidence: By placing Apache in front of the legacy server, the organization can terminate SSL/TLS connections at the proxy, inject required security headers, and forward requests to the internal repository over a secure tunnel, shielding the legacy infrastructure from direct exposure.

options: The proxy cannot handle more than ten concurrent users.
The proxy introduces latency and acts as a potential single point of failure.
The proxy requires a complete rewrite of the legacy application code.
The proxy is incompatible with standard HTTPS protocols.
